text: This job was never yours.
Not because of your skills.
Because of a visa nobody told you about.
Bengaluru. Eleven forty-seven at night.
A software engineer is sending her best
application to Berlin.
It's dead on arrival.
That job was never open to her.
Job boards are built for volume.
Search. Click. Apply. Repeat.
But across borders, volume is the problem.
That listing needs a work permit you don't
have. The company won't sponsor a visa.
And the match score never tells you.
So you apply everywhere.
You hear nothing back.
And you slowly burn your name with recruiters.
It isn't a skills problem.
It's an information problem.
So we built Skylark.
A job application service that only puts you
forward for roles you can actually take.
It explains every decision.
And a human checks everything before it's sent.
One profile. Upload your resume,
and Skylark pulls out your headline,
skills and experience.
Every field is checked on the server.
Skills against a curated taxonomy,
Stack Overflow tags and the European ESCO
catalogue. Even your email domain is verified.
Your dashboard: new matches, active
applications, today's progress.
Open any role and see exactly why it fits.
Seven factors, each with a score and a
sentence you can read.
Hit apply, and AI drafts a tailored resume and
cover letter. Every change comes with a
reason. Nothing is applied until you accept it.
Then a real person takes over.
They run a five-point checklist,
submit the application, and record the
employer's confirmation reference.
And you watch it all on your tracker.
Saved. Applied. Interview.
Now, under the hood.
Listings stream in from public job APIs:
Arbeitnow, sixteen Greenhouse company boards,
and others when they're configured.
Raw HTML becomes clean fields:
title, seniority, location, salary,
sponsorship and skills.
A SHA-256 fingerprint kills duplicates.
Stale listings get closed.
And if nothing refreshes for twenty-four
hours, candidates are told.
Then the match engine scores every role
against you.
Skills carry thirty percent.
Eligibility, twenty.
Experience, eighteen.
Location, twelve.
Sponsorship, eight.
Preferences, seven.
Education, five.
The score is their weighted sum.
And here's the rule that changes everything.
If a role won't sponsor someone who needs it,
the score is capped at thirty-five.
However good your skills look,
a job you can't legally take will never
outrank one you can.
The whole product is one Next.js app:
the website, the candidate app,
an operations console and a shared inbox.
Every service talks to one repository
interface. In production, that's Supabase
Postgres, with row-level security on every table.
No credentials? The same interface runs on a
seeded in-memory store.
The whole product works on a laptop,
with zero setup.
Security isn't assumed.
It's tested. The test suite runs every
migration on a real Postgres engine,
and proves one candidate can never read
another's data.
AI sits behind an interface too.
Claude drafts the tailoring, its output is
validated against a schema, and if the model
is unavailable, a deterministic rules engine takes over.
Background work runs through a queue.
Every task carries an idempotency key,
no two workers claim the same job,
and failures back off before they're set aside.
And it's live today, at skylarkgo.in.
Live job listings.
Google sign-in. Chat-style onboarding.
Subscriptions in rupees through Razorpay.
And a specialist review queue with a
twenty-four hour target.
Next: more job sources for India,
and matching every candidate against the
entire catalogue.
Skylark doesn't try to send more applications.
It tries to send the right ones,
and to show you why.
Fewer applications.
Better reasons. And a person checking every one.
Skylark. Your next move, already in motion.
